title: Apparitions and private revelation (CCC 67)
hook: no apparition is required belief, even approved ones

segments.voice: Yesterday, Częstochowa: a Black Madonna with sword cuts on her cheek, and a legend about Saint Luke that Catholics may hold lightly. Your line was the scarred icon. What marks did you leave alone? Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

A woman at a parish fish fry says, between bites, that she's never been sure about Lourdes. The man across from her nearly drops his fork. Doesn't the Church approve it? Isn't that part of being Catholic? It's a fair question, and the next days of this path make it urgent, because they visit places where people say Mary appeared: a grotto in France, a field in Portugal, a church wall in Ireland, a school in Rwanda, a forest in Vietnam. Before we go, we need the rule the Church uses for all of them. It's short, it's in the Catechism, and it may surprise the man with the fork. Today's word is the name for what those visions are.
screen: `NEVER SURE ABOUT LOURDES.` → `PLACES WHERE PEOPLE SAY MARY APPEARED.` → `FIRST, THE RULE.`

segments.voice: Begin with what the Church calls public revelation. The Letter to the Hebrews opens by saying God spoke in many ways through the prophets, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "last of all, in these days hath spoken to us by his Son." The Catechism draws the conclusion: in Christ, God has said everything. No new public revelation is to be expected before Christ comes again. That's the faith the whole Church holds and hands on. Then comes paragraph sixty-seven, and the other kind. Over the centuries, it says, there have been so-called private revelations, some of them recognized by the Church's authority. Private doesn't mean secret; a crowd might see it. It means they don't belong to the deposit of faith. Their job, the Catechism says, isn't to improve Christ's revelation or complete it. It's to help people live by it more fully in a particular time. Next, what approval means. When the Church looks into a reported apparition and approves it, it is saying, in effect: nothing here contradicts the faith, and you may honor it. It is not saying that every Catholic is bound to believe it happened. The woman at the fish fry is free to stay unsure. The man is free to make a pilgrimage. Neither one is a better Catholic for it. Last, the attitude. Paul gives one to an early church: "Despise not prophecies. But prove all things; hold fast that which is good." Not scorn. Not swallowing everything. Testing, and keeping what's good. That's how Catholics are asked to walk into the stories ahead.
screen: `IN CHRIST, GOD HAS SAID EVERYTHING.` · `PRIVATE: OUTSIDE THE DEPOSIT OF FAITH.` · `APPROVED MEANS PERMITTED, NOT REQUIRED.` · `TEST IT, KEEP WHAT'S GOOD.` · then, large: `PROVE ALL THINGS; HOLD FAST THAT WHICH IS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold such stories humbly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a story you've heard of a vision, a healing, a sign: from church, from family, from the news. Notice which way you lean. Toward it, wanting it to be true? Away from it, ready to roll your eyes? Neither lean is wrong. Just notice it, and set it down. Then hold the story the way you'd hold something fragile that belongs to someone else: open hand, no squeezing. If you pray, you can ask for the grace to keep what's good. The bell holds the time.
Private revelation. A vision or message, even a public one, that isn't part of the faith the whole Church must believe. It can help people live the Gospel; it can never add to it. Today's word.
Your line: never required. Today, when a story is offered as proof of anything, test it gently, and keep what's good in it. Day one thousand three hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church distinguishes public revelation, completed in Christ, from private revelations such as approved apparitions; Catholics may honor approved apparitions and visit their shrines, but are not required to believe in them.

fork.reveal: no apparition is required belief, even an approved one. private revelations are outside the deposit of faith; approval permits honoring them, it doesn't oblige.

original.note: Greek: revelation, the word that names the last book of the Bible, which the Douay-Rheims calls the Apocalypse.

what it means: a private revelation can help people live the Gospel; it never adds to it, and it's never required.
what a scholar hears: CCC 65–67: public revelation is complete in Christ; private revelations, even recognized ones, stand outside the deposit of faith.

notes: Editor: changed 'a hillside in Rwanda' to 'a school in Rwanda' to match day 1348 (the Kibeho visionaries were schoolgirls); otherwise unchanged.

CCC 65–67 paraphrased (God has said everything in the Word; no new public revelation before Christ's glorious manifestation; private revelations, some recognized, do not belong to the deposit of faith; their role is to help live more fully by Christ's revelation in a certain period). The Catechism's wording is copyrighted, so nothing is quoted.

The description of what approval means ('nothing contradicts the faith, and you may honor it', not 'you must believe') is a general summary; the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith's 2024 norms use new terms (e.g. nihil obstat). Confirm the summary is fair.
The hook lists places the coming days visit (France, Portugal, Ireland, Rwanda, Vietnam); Guadalupe and Vailankanni also follow. Confirm the framing.
Douay-Rheims wording of Hebrews 1:2 and 1 Thessalonians 5:20–21: confirm.
Original: ἀποκάλυψις as the Greek for revelation; confirm pronunciation.
